corrected_proposal.title: Trump Hosts Baltic Leaders and Reaffirms U.S. Partnership
corrected_proposal.description_short: Trump welcomed Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania’s leaders at an April 3, 2018 summit and publicly reaffirmed U.S. partnership.
corrected_proposal.description_medium: At a White House working lunch and U.S.-Baltic Centennial Summit on April 3, 2018, President Trump welcomed the leaders of Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania. He congratulated the countries on their independence centennials and publicly affirmed a renewed partnership and U.S. recognition of their sovereignty. The original synopsis’s alleged private remark to aides that the leaders were “all the same” is not substantiated by this public transcript.
corrected_proposal.description_long: On April 3, 2018, President Donald Trump received the leaders of Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania at the White House for a working lunch and the U.S.-Baltic Centennial Summit. Trump congratulated the three countries on the 100th anniversary of their independence and said he was honored to host them. In his remarks, he said the United States had never ceased recognizing the sovereignty of the three Baltic republics and added, “we never let you down. And we won’t let you down.” He described the summit as renewing a partnership grounded in sovereignty and respect for the rule of law. His remarks also previewed discussions about bilateral trade, investment, and military-equipment purchases. The archived transcript supports this public meeting and the statements made there. It does not include the private “all the same” comment attributed to Trump in the original synopsis, and targeted searches did not corroborate that quotation. This narrowed record preserves the documented summit while removing the unsupported private allegation and the inference that it showed indifference to NATO commitments. The transcript does not record private conversations.

Remarks by President Trump Before a Working Lunch with Heads of the Baltic States

Issued on: April 3, 2018

PRESIDENT TRUMP: Today, it’s my pleasure to congratulate Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania on the 100th anniversary of their independence. That’s really quite a great achievement, and congratulations. And I’m honored to have you with us in the White House and the Oval Office.

From the very beginning of your countries’ independence, the United States never — and this is, like, never — and I think you know that better than anybody — never ceased to recognize the sovereignty of the three Baltic republics, even though, throughout the years, there’s been a lot of conflict, a lot of problems, a lot of difficulty, and we never let you down. And we won’t let you down.

At today’s U.S.-Baltic Centennial Summit, we’re inaugurating 100 years of renewed partnership among our nations, grounded once more in our shared commitment to independent sovereignty and a total respect of the rule of law.

This afternoon, we will discuss our cooperation on a range of issues, including expanding bilateral trade and investment.

corrected_proposal.title: NPR Reported DOGE Staff Had Nuclear Network Accounts; DOE Said They Were Never Used
corrected_proposal.description_short: NPR reported two DOGE employees had accounts on classified nuclear networks; DOE said the accounts were never activated or accessed.
corrected_proposal.description_medium: An NPR report published April 28, 2025 said two DOGE employees had accounts on classified networks used for nuclear information. The Department of Energy said the accounts had never been activated or accessed. NPR also explained that an account’s presence on a network did not by itself grant access to classified data. The reporting documents an account-creation and oversight concern, not confirmed viewing or extraction of nuclear files.
corrected_proposal.description_long: On April 28, 2025, NPR reported that two Department of Government Efficiency employees had accounts on classified networks used by the National Nuclear Security Administration and the Defense Department. NPR cited two sources who said the accounts had been present for at least two weeks. The Department of Energy first denied that the employees had accessed the networks, then said the accounts had been created but never activated or accessed. NPR also reported that merely appearing on a network directory would not by itself give an employee access to classified data stored there. The supported event is the creation and listing of the accounts, followed by reporting about them and the department’s explanation. The reporting does not establish that either employee viewed, copied, or otherwise accessed nuclear weapons information. It also does not establish the frozen entry’s claims of an unauthorized file breach, foreign business conflicts, or an immediate federal investigation. This repair narrows the entry to the documented access-control concern and preserves the agency’s response.

corrected_proposal.title: Trump Reinstates Schedule F as Schedule Policy/Career
corrected_proposal.description_short: Trump's January 20, 2025 executive order reinstated Schedule F under the name Schedule Policy/Career.
corrected_proposal.description_medium: On January 20, 2025, Donald Trump signed an executive order immediately reinstating the 2020 Schedule F order and renaming the category “Schedule Policy/Career.” The order directed the Office of Personnel Management to amend regulations and issue guidance on additional positions for agencies to consider. It establishes a federal workforce policy directive; it does not show how many employees were later reclassified or removed.
corrected_proposal.description_long: On January 20, 2025, President Donald Trump signed “Restoring Accountability to Policy-Influencing Positions Within the Federal Workforce.” Section 2 immediately reinstated Executive Order 13957, the 2020 order creating Schedule F, subject to amendments in the new order. Those amendments replaced the excepted-service schedule label “F” with “Policy/Career” and directed the Office of Personnel Management to amend regulations that could impede implementation. The order also directed OPM to issue, within 30 days, guidance about additional position categories agencies should consider recommending for inclusion. It says employees in or applicants for these positions need not personally or politically support the President, but are required to faithfully implement administration policies; failure to do so is grounds for dismissal. These are the signed order’s rules and directions. The accessed document does not establish how many positions were later reclassified, how many employees lost protections, or whether any specific person was dismissed under it. This record describes the enacted policy mechanism, not a completed workforce purge or an asserted list of political enemies.

corrected_proposal.title: Kennedy Removes All 17 Members of CDC Vaccine Advisory Committee
corrected_proposal.description_short: On June 9, 2025, Robert F. Kennedy Jr. removed all 17 members of CDC’s vaccine advisory committee, ACIP.
corrected_proposal.description_medium: On June 9, 2025, HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. removed all 17 sitting members of the CDC’s Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP), which advises CDC on vaccine safety, efficacy, and clinical need. HHS said replacements were under consideration. Reuters reported that the move drew protest from vaccine scientists; available sources do not establish later changes in recommendations or health outcomes.
corrected_proposal.description_long:
On June 9, 2025, HHS announced that Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. had removed all 17 sitting members of the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices, the CDC advisory committee that makes recommendations about vaccine safety, efficacy, and clinical need. HHS said new members were under consideration and framed the decision as an effort to restore public trust in vaccines.

Reuters reported that the entire 17-member panel was being replaced and that many vaccine scientists protested the move. HHS said the members had been appointed during the Biden administration, including 13 in 2024, and argued that without their removal the Trump administration would not have been able to choose a committee majority until 2028. These are the agency’s stated rationale and reported reaction. The sources establish the committee’s removal, but they do not show what recommendations followed or measure any resulting change in vaccine uptake, safety, or health outcomes. This entry records the personnel and advisory-structure change without treating the agency’s rationale or critics’ concerns as a proven public-health consequence.

corrected_proposal.description_long: This corrected entry records a February 2025 change in senior U.S. military leadership. Reuters reported that President Donald Trump fired Joint Chiefs of Staff Chairman Gen. C.Q. Brown on February 21 and described five other admirals and generals as pushed out in the same shake-up. The Associated Press reported that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth followed Brown’s dismissal by firing Navy Adm. Lisa Franchetti, then chief of naval operations, and Air Force Gen. James Slife, vice chief of the Air Force; AP also reported on changes to the services’ top military lawyers. The supplied record asserted that officers were removed because they testified against Trump in impeachment proceedings. The reporting reviewed for this corrected card documents who was dismissed, but does not establish that causal allegation or identify impeachment testimony as the reason. The account therefore names only the documented personnel actions and leaves motive unresolved. It does not characterize the changes as retaliation, a purge of witnesses, or proof of political loyalty. No conclusion about legality or resulting readiness effects is drawn. This correction preserves the dated leadership-change event while removing unsupported participants and motive.

corrected_proposal.description_medium: The Associated Press reported that Pam Bondi was sworn in as attorney general on February 5, 2025, and hours later called for a Justice Department “weaponization working group.” AP said the group would scrutinize Jack Smith’s work and review prosecutions stemming from January 6. corrected_proposal.description_long: On February 5, 2025, the Associated Press reported that Pam Bondi was sworn in as attorney general and, hours later, called for a Justice Department “weaponization working group.” AP said the group would scrutinize the work of special counsel Jack Smith, who had charged Donald Trump in two criminal cases, and review what Bondi described as “unethical prosecutions” stemming from the January 6, 2021 attack on the Capitol. The supplied original entry instead claimed that Bondi ordered DOJ to drop or suspend a broad set of cases against Trump allies on January 20, including fraud and campaign-finance matters. The date is incompatible with AP’s account of Bondi taking office on February 5, and the AP article describes reviews rather than case dismissals. This correction records the same-day directive AP documents and does not claim that cases were dismissed. It also does not treat the act of reviewing cases as proof of misconduct. The record does not establish which cases, if any, the working group later recommended for action or what outcomes followed.

corrected_proposal.title: Trump promoted a $59.99 branded Bible; $300 million in revenue is unsupported
corrected_proposal.description_short: Trump promoted the $59.99 God Bless the USA Bible; AP reporting does not substantiate the $300 million revenue claim.
corrected_proposal.description_medium: On March 26, 2024, Trump promoted the God Bless the USA Bible and urged supporters to buy it from a website listing the price at $59.99. AP later reported close to 120,000 copies shipped to the United States from China by late March and estimated about $7 million in potential retail sales at the minimum price. AP also cited a disclosure showing $300,000 in CIC Ventures Bible royalties, while noting the period and any additional payments were unclear. The $300 million revenue claim is unsupported by these reports.
corrected_proposal.description_long:
On March 26, 2024, Donald Trump promoted the “God Bless the USA Bible,” urging supporters to buy it from a website listing the price at $59.99. The website said Trump’s name and image were used under a paid license from CIC Ventures, a company he reported owning. The book combined a King James Version Bible with U.S. founding documents and the Pledge of Allegiance.

The original title’s $300 million revenue figure is not substantiated by the reporting reviewed here. In October 2024, the Associated Press reported that trade records showed close to 120,000 copies shipped from China to the United States between early February and late March. At the minimum retail price, AP estimated potential sales revenue for those shipments at about $7 million. AP also cited a financial disclosure showing $300,000 in Bible royalties earned by CIC Ventures, while stating that the disclosure period and any additional payments were unclear. Shipment estimates, potential retail sales, company royalties, and Trump’s total receipts are different measures; these reports do not establish total eventual sales or payments. The corrected entry records the promotion and licensing arrangement, removes the unsupported $300 million claim, and leaves final revenue and total royalties unknown.

corrected_proposal.title: Trump Pardoned Three Former Border Patrol Agents in December 2020
corrected_proposal.description_short: Trump pardoned former Border Patrol agents Ignacio Ramos, Jose Compean and Gary Brugman in December 2020.
corrected_proposal.description_medium: Trump pardoned Ignacio Ramos and Jose Compean on December 22, 2020, and Gary Brugman on December 23. The White House and Texas Tribune sources describe their separate convictions involving assault or deprivation of civil rights. The January 2025 clemency proclamation concerned January 6-related offenses, so the original date is corrected to the documented 2020 actions.
corrected_proposal.description_long: President Donald Trump granted full pardons to former Border Patrol agents Ignacio Ramos and Jose Compean on December 22, 2020, and former agent Gary Brugman on December 23. The archived White House statement about Ramos and Compean says they were convicted of assault, a firearm offense and deprivation of civil rights in connection with the 2005 shooting of a man near the U.S.-Mexico border. A Texas Tribune report describes Brugman’s 2002 conviction for deprivation of rights after he struck detained migrants; the report says he served more than two years in federal prison. These grants occurred in December 2020, not as part of Trump’s January 20, 2025 clemency proclamation. The Justice Department describes that later proclamation as covering offenses relating to the January 6, 2021 Capitol events. This correction preserves the earlier pardons and the documented conviction records while removing the unsupported claim that the agents were pardoned in January 2025 or that all cited cases were the same event. It does not infer why Trump granted clemency or state that the convictions were later vacated.
